To hoist something means to lift it upward, usually with effort, and often using a rope, chain, pulley, crane, or some other mechanical tool. The key idea is that the thing being lifted is heavy, large, or awkward enough that you can't just pick it up with your bare hands the way you'd pick up a pencil. There is a sense of deliberate, effortful raising.

Think of a sailor pulling a rope to raise a flag to the top of a tall pole. That's hoisting. The flag goes up, hand over hand, rope by rope, until it reaches the top and flies proudly. That physical image — something being pulled upward, purposefully and with some exertion — is the heart of the word.

These three words are close cousins, but hoist has its own personality.

Lift is the most general word. You can lift a feather, lift a finger, lift a baby. It asks nothing about how heavy the object is or how you're doing it.

Raise is also general. You raise your hand, raise the volume, raise a child. It focuses on the result (something goes higher) more than the effort.

Hoist is more specific. It quietly suggests:

  • The object is heavy or unwieldy.
  • The action requires real effort or mechanical assistance.
  • The movement is upward (not sideways).
  • There is often a sense of displaying the object once it's at the top.

So while you'd lift a cup off a table and raise your eyebrows, you'd hoist a heavy crate onto a truck or hoist a flag up a pole.

1. Flags and Banners

This is perhaps the most classic use. Countries, ships, and teams hoist their flags — they raise them up a pole or mast, usually as a symbol of pride, identity, or authority.

The soldiers hoisted the national flag at dawn.

2. Ships and Sailing

On ships, sailors hoist sails, cargo, and anchors. Because ships deal with very heavy equipment and require ropes and pulleys to move things, "hoist" fits naturally.

The crew hoisted the sails as the wind picked up.
The crane hoisted the cargo container onto the deck.

3. Heavy Objects and Construction

At building sites or warehouses, workers hoist beams, crates, machines, and equipment using cranes or pulleys.

Workers hoisted the steel beam to the top floor.

4. A Person's Own Body

Sometimes, a person hoists themselves up onto something — a wall, a ledge, a bar — implying they heave their own weight upward with effort.

He grabbed the ledge and hoisted himself up onto the roof.
She hoisted herself out of the swimming pool.

5. Lifting a Glass (Informal/Festive)

In a casual or celebratory context, people sometimes say someone hoisted a glass — meaning they raised a drink for a toast. This is a light, somewhat playful use.

They hoisted their glasses and toasted to the new year.

An important shade of meaning: hoist carries weight (pun intended). When you use this word, you're telling your reader that the lifting wasn't casual or easy. Compare:

  • She lifted the book off the table. → Easy, ordinary.
  • She hoisted the box onto the shelf. → Heavy, required effort.

If you describe someone hoisting something light, it would sound odd or even humorous, because the word sets an expectation of struggle.

Here are the natural ways "hoist" appears in sentences:

  • Hoist + object: They hoisted the anchor.
  • Hoist + object + up: He hoisted the bag up onto his shoulder.
  • Hoist + object + onto/over/into: The workers hoisted the engine into the truck.
  • Hoist + yourself + up/onto/over: She hoisted herself up over the fence.
The Famous Idiom: "Hoist by Your Own Petard"

You will likely come across this phrase one day, so it's worth knowing. It means to be harmed, trapped, or defeated by your own plan or trick — essentially, your scheme backfires and hurts you instead of the person you were targeting.

A "petard" was a small explosive device used in old warfare to blow open doors or walls. If it went off too early, the engineer who set it could be "hoisted" (blown upward) by his own bomb. The phrase preserves that dark irony beautifully.

He tried to spread rumors about his rival, but the truth came out and he ended up being hoisted by his own petard — his own reputation was destroyed instead.

You might also see the modern variation "hoist with your own petard" — both mean the same thing.

ConceptDetail

To hoist is to lift something heavy upward, typically with rope, a machine, or significant bodily effort. It's most at home with flags on poles, cargo on ships, and heavy loads at construction sites, but it also works when a person heaves their own body up onto something. It's always upward, always effortful, and often implies the object is being raised to a position where it will be seen, used, or secured. The key idiom to remember is "hoist by your own petard" — your plan blows up in your face.
